text:
Research supports testing the training objective before adding more gating, but does not establish superiority for NextItNet specifically. [Sampled Softmax for Item Recommendation (TOIS 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.02327) identifies model-agnostic benefits: implicit hard-negative emphasis, popularity-bias mitigation, and ranking-metric connections; it also warns that cosine normalization can limit representation-magnitude learning. [Scalable Cross-Entropy (RecSys 2024)](https://dspace.mit.edu/entities/publication/5392aca9-0bae-4176-9b3a-a8165957ba26) approximates softmax using informative catalog subsets retrieved through maximum-inner-product search. However, [a 2024 sequential-recommendation sampling study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds substantial dataset-dependent accuracy and popularity tradeoffs. Harder negatives are not uniformly better.

A suitable experiment—an inference from these findings—is to preserve the causal dilated-convolution NextItNet and replace single-negative training with multi-negative sampled cross-entropy: log(1 + Σ exp((s_negative − s_positive)/temperature)). Compare uniform candidates against a uniform/semi-hard mixture mined using the same network; exclude padding, the target, and observed training positives, and deduplicate candidates. Warm up with uniform sampling before increasing hardness. Unobserved items remain uncertain negatives, so avoid automatically treating the highest-scoring items as reliable negatives. Tune temperature and negative count separately, selecting solely by fixed macro validation HR@10; this loss is a ranking surrogate, not an exact HR@10 objective. A [2026 preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11061) finds that larger batches with fewer negatives can outperform the reverse under fixed memory assumptions, supporting budget-matched comparisons rather than maximizing negative count. All sampling and loss changes can operate within one jointly trained model per category.
